anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between physical data model (tables, partitions, indexes, data types, constraints) and the workload’s access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths irrespective of optimizer statistics.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Accumulation of obsolete row versions and rollback records that background vacuum/cleanup workers cannot reclaim quickly enough, inflating table size and visibility-check cost.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The write-ahead log pipeline (generation, flushing, switching, archiving, retention) is saturated, elongating commit latency and stalling further DML.

When all three root causes coexist, the database exhibits compound symptoms: queries read far more pages because poorly designed or missing indexes push them into full scans over bloat-inflated heaps and indexes; each scan must traverse long version chains, increasing CPU and buffer-pool pressure. Concurrently, the excessive DML generated by design flaws (e.g., unneeded secondary-index maintenance, hot-spot primary keys) and by MVCC cleanup work produces a surge in redo that overwhelms the log buffer and log file subsystem, manifesting as rising commit times, frequent log flush waits, and delayed checkpoints. Background vacuum or garbage-collection workers stay perpetually active yet fall further behind because their own delete and prune operations add additional redo and contend for the same clogged log and I/O channels. End-user sessions experience a mix of slow queries, unpredictable latency spikes, and occasional write stalls when log space or transaction-ID horizons are exhausted.

Causally, the poor schema and index design increases the volume and cost of both reads and writes—more non-covering index lookups, more page splits, and heavier update/delete churn—thereby accelerating row-version creation. The surging version count bloats table and index pages, worsening scan performance and causing still more I/O that must be logged. Simultaneously, every extra page modification and every MVCC cleanup action emits additional log records, pushing the transaction-log subsystem past its throughput budget. The saturated log path then slows commit acknowledgment, lengthening transaction lifetimes, which in turn widens the snapshot horizon and delays version reclamation. This feedback loop reinforces each anomaly, quickly degrading overall OLTP performance and stability.

entry.official_definition: Aborts any statement that takes more than the specified amount of time; zero disables the timeout.
entry.trigger_condition: A SQL statement runs longer than statement_timeout, measured from command arrival until completion.
entry.workload_impact: The running statement is aborted; when configured, the timed-out statement is logged.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when statement execution exceeds a configured execution-time budget because the operation runs too long or the workload is blocked behind other work.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect query shape, access path quality, resource contention, and whether the timeout threshold should be reviewed together with the workload pattern.
